title: Lard & olive bar soap
subtitle: A firm, long-lasting bar with a quiet lather
excerpt: Cold-process bar soap made with lard and olive oil. The lard gives a hard, white bar with a creamy, conditioning lather; the olive brings extra moisturising quality and keeps the bar mild. Yields eight bars; hardens in 4-6 weeks.
sourceNotes: Anne Bramson, Soap: Making It, Enjoying It (1972), traditional lard-based formulations and Castile comparisons. Susan Miller Cavitch, The Soapmaker's Companion (1997), SAP values for lard and olive oil, cure-time guidance. Soap-Calc SAP table (accessed 2026), NaOH values: lard 0.138, olive oil 0.134. USDA AAS oil-fatty-acid data for lard tallow composition.

recipe.batchNotes: Scale only after running the new weights through a SAP calculator. Lard SAP is 0.138; olive is 0.134. Any change in oil ratio changes the lye requirement.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bars cure fully in 6 weeks and improve for up to a year in a cool, airy cupboard. Make a large batch ahead, the bars only get better.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: 2 years or more in a cool, dry cupboard on a ventilated rack. Discard if orange spots appear on the cut face (DOS, rancid superfat oil) or if the bar develops a sharp, paint-like smell.

glossaryTerms.definition: The chemical reaction between fat and sodium hydroxide (lye) that produces soap and glycerol. Each fat has a SAP value, the grams of NaOH needed to fully convert one gram of that fat.
The percentage of oil left unsaponified in a finished bar, giving a skin-conditioning quality. A 5% superfat means 5% of the oil weight remains as free fatty acids in the cured bar.
The point at which the soap batter thickens enough to hold a trail on its surface when drizzled, the signal that emulsification is complete and the batter is ready to mould.

content.text: Lard and olive bar soap is a mild, hard-wearing bar built on two of the oldest soap-making fats. The lard, rendered pig fat, gives a bright white, dense bar with a fine, conditioning lather; the olive oil softens the bar slightly and adds slip on the skin. Together they sit at about a 60:40 ratio by weight, with a 5% superfat to keep the finished bar gentle. The bars cure for 4-6 weeks and keep for two years.
Ingredients

items.prepNote: rendered pork lard; 60% of oil weight; gives a dense, white, conditioning bar
pure (not extra virgin); 40% of oil weight; adds conditioning slip
NaOH at 99% purity; calculated for 5% superfat; add lye to water, never water to lye
32% of oil weight; the lye solution liquid

content.text: Method
Make the lye solution
Put on protective gloves and goggles before handling lye. Work in a well-ventilated space, near an open window or outdoors.
Weigh the distilled water into the HDPE pitcher. Weigh the sodium hydroxide separately.

Pour the lye into the water in a steady stream, stirring with a stainless-steel spoon. Never add water to lye, the violent reaction can splatter caustic liquid. The solution heats to around 80°C immediately and gives off fumes; do not lean over the pitcher.
Set the pitcher somewhere safe and let it cool to 38-42°C, about 30-40 minutes.
Prepare the oils
If the lard is solid, melt it gently in a saucepan over a low heat, then remove from the heat and add the olive oil. The blended oils should sit at 38-42°C, the same range as the lye solution.
Blend to trace
Pour the lye solution into the oil pot in a thin, steady stream, stirring as you go.
Use the stick blender in short bursts, 5 seconds on, 5 seconds off, stirring between bursts. Lard-based batters
trace
quickly (sometimes within 2 minutes). Stop as soon as the batter holds a light trail on its surface.
Mould and unmould
Pour the batter into the silicone loaf mould and smooth the top. Cover with a sheet of baking paper, then wrap the mould in a towel to insulate it.
Leave for 24-48 hours. The batter goes through a gel phase, it will look translucent and darker for a while, then lighten as it cools. This is normal.
Unmould onto a sheet of baking paper. The bar should feel firm and no longer sticky. If it's still soft, leave it in the mould for another 24 hours.
Cut into 8 bars with a sharp knife. Wear gloves, fresh soap is still caustic until fully cured.
Cure
Space the cut bars on a rack so air can circulate around each one. Keep them in a cool, dry place out of direct sunlight.
Turn the bars every 2 weeks so each side dries evenly.
At 4 weeks, test a corner of one bar with the tip of your tongue, if it gives a mild 'zap' like a 9-volt battery, the
saponification
is not yet complete. Continue curing.
At 6 weeks, the bars are ready. The
superfat
oils condition skin on washing and the lather is dense and creamy.
Storage and shelf life

Keep cured bars on a ventilated rack in a cool, dry cupboard. They keep well for 2 years. Discard any bar that develops orange spots on the cut face (DOS, rancid superfat) or a sharp smell. In use, keep the bar on a draining soap dish so it dries between washes.
